extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory, philosophy of humor, and comedy practitioners interested in formal principles of the comic
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Bergson's formal principles for how sentences, situations, and characters become comic; useful for analyzing or constructing humor in literature and performance. Focuses on mechanisms (repetition, inversion, transposition), comic language, and comic character conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic transformation of sentences (three laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrase becomes comic if, though reversed, it still makes sense; if it expresses two independent sets of ideas; or if it transposes an idea into a key other than its own. These are the three fundamental laws of THE COMIC TRANSFORMATION OF SENTENCES: repetition (applied to events), INVERSION, and RECIPROCAL INTERFERENCE, with TRANSPOSITION occupying a central role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the three operations (inversion, reciprocal interference, transposition) to series of words as one does to series of events; examples follow in subsequent entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (of sentence elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Switching grammatical roles (e.g., subject for object and vice versa) to obtain a new, comic meaning. INVERSION is the least interesting but easily applied device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by wits to refute ideas humorously; example: a neighbour retorts, 'What do you mean by putting your terrace under my pipe?' (Labiche). Useful for quick, repartee-style jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference / pun and play upon words
rubrics_metrics.description: Bracketing two independent meanings in the same expression so they interfere with one another. The pun is the least reputable form (different sentences with same sound); the true play upon words uses one sentence to express two sets of ideas via a word's multiple meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish pun (homophony) from genuine play on words (single sentence, figurative vs literal meanings). Play upon words often betrays a 'LAPSE OF ATTENTION' in language and is amusing for that negligent quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition (key-shift of expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposing the natural expression of an idea into another key always produces a comic effect: rendering an idea in a style or setting foreign to its 'natural' expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No need to present both natural and transposed forms; the audience supplies the natural one. Transposition ranges from buffoonery to subtle humour and is compared to repetition in comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody (solemn into familiar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposing the solemn into the familiar—using commonplace or modern terms for lofty subjects—produces parody. Example: describing dawn 'like a lobster being boiled' (Jean Paul Richter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody can also operate by expressing 'old-world matters in terms of modern life' to comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degradation as comic transposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating something formerly dignified as mean or trivial (degradation) is one form of transposition that produces laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers who define the comic as degradation capture only one aspect; degradation is a subset of transposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (small spoken of as large)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speaking of small things as though they were large (physical transposition) produces comic exaggeration when prolonged or systematic—e.g., mock-heroic mode and methodical braggadocio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration is especially comic when it is sustained and systematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upward transposition of moral value (respectable language for disreputable matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing disreputable or low-class matters in the language of 'respectability' is comic. The intensity of the effect may not depend on length; a single word can reveal a system of transposition (example from Gogol: 'Your peculations are too extensive for an official of your rank').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly characteristic in English literature (Dickens, Thackeray); this reveals a 'moral organisation of immorality.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Real vs ideal transposition: irony and humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition between the real and the ideal yields two distinct modes: IRONY—stating what ought to be and pretending it is; HUMOUR—describing accurately what is and pretending it ought to be. Irony is oratorical; humour is scientific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour delights in concrete, technical details and is 'a moralist disguised as a scientist'; irony emphasizes the aspirational ideal and can become fervent eloquence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of professional jargon / business phraseology as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposing everyday ideas into a profession's technical vocabulary, or extending business phrases to social relations, creates comic effects (e.g., 'Your kindness of the third ult.' parodying 'Your favour of the third instant').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be deepened when it reveals a character fault (treating marriage as business in Labiche plays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lapse of attention in language as source of comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Play upon words makes us think of a 'negligence on the part of language'—a momentary lapse of attention—producing amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic arises from language's failure to perform its 'real function' (accommodate itself to things), thus allowing words to accommodate things to themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as social corrective (unsociability focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter has a social meaning: it reproves absentmindedness and lack of adaptability; any individual who automatically goes his own way without adjusting to society is comic. Laughter functions as a kind of social 'ragging' aimed to humiliate/correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic targets UNSOCIABILITY rather than immoral conduct per se; the face of comedy is social discipline rather than mere ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incompatibility of laughter with emotion (must not arouse feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: For something (even a serious vice) to be laughable it MUST NOT AROUSE OUR FEELINGS; laughter appeals to intelligence and is incompatible with sympathy, pity, or fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic poets use techniques to prevent spectator sympathy (see 'isolating the feeling' below) so that vices or serious matters can become ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolating the feeling (parasitic emotion) to prevent sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: One method to render a feeling non-contagious is to depict it as isolated within the character—'a parasitic organism'—rigid and not harmonising with other mental states, so it fails to elicit audience sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a feeling remains compartmentalized and does not impregnate the character's other states (no harmonics), the emotion does not become dramatic and thus can be comic (example: Harpagon forgetting the dramatic meeting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct attention to gestures rather than actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy directs attention to gestures (attitudes, movements, automatic language) rather than to actions (intentional, conscious behaviour). Gestures are automatic and 'explosive' and prevent us from taking things seriously; actions invite drama and sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make a character comic emphasise puppet-like movements, habitual attitudes, or automatic phrases (Tartuffe entering with ritual words) rather than consequential actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatism / absentmindedness as essential comic condition
rubrics_metrics.description: What is essentially laughable is what is done automatically: involuntary gestures, unconscious remarks, systematic absentmindedness. The deeper the absentmindedness, the higher the comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effects often arise when a character contradicts themselves unawares (examples: philosophers angrily losing control after preaching calm; Vadius producing poetry after ridiculing poets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity and ready-made behavior produce comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechanical, ready-made, or stereotyped element of personality (rigidity) is comic when contrasted with supple, living behaviour. Habitual, mechanistic responses invite imitation and ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigidity makes one a type; the more a person crystallises into a 'stock character,' the more comic they become.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic characters are types (generality over individuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy's objective is to depict general types—the ready-made element in personality—so that resemblance to a type has something comic in it and producing stock characters is central to comedy's purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy is the only art that aims at the general; making a character a 'type' allows others to fall into the same category and be laughed at by association.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic depends on failing to arouse individual sympathy (selection/labeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because life simplifies reality for practical use, language and perception emphasize genera over individuality. This selection and labelling (reading the 'labels' affixed to things) strips individuality and predisposes us to find the general, stereotyped aspects comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of generic words and conventional labels helps reduce individuality and thus contributes to comic effect; the comic exploits this categorical simplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between comedy and drama: action vs gesture, generality vs individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama concentrates on action and the integration of character and situation to elicit sympathy; comedy emphasises gestures, automatism, and types, so characters could survive a change of situation and still be recognisable as comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building or assessing comic scenes, ensure that characters display isolated, habitual gestures and general types rather than integrated, situation-specific actions.
